0.trueWording: the natural voice for the story teller
0.note: Aidan Moher raw page reached (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Both limbs on page: 'To me, the first person voice is the natural voice for the story teller. We use it often when we are telling family and friends what happened to day' (page's own typo for 'today').

1.trueWording: privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings
1.note: Quote exact and complete on the raw page: 'With first person, the reader gets to know the viewpoint character intimately because the reader is privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings.'

2.trueWording: see what is coming even if the main character doesn't
2.note: SFFWorld raw page reached (HTTP 200). Both limbs on page: 'The reader can only know exactly as much as the protagonist knows' and 'the reader will perhaps be able to see what is coming even if the main character doesn't.' Claim's 'may' preserves the page's 'perhaps' hedge.

3.trueWording: little prologues at the beginning of each chapter
3.note: Quote exact. Purpose limb supported in the same paragraph: 'the writer is limited to telling the reader what that character knows at that moment... In Farseer, I coped with that by having little prologues at the beginning of each chapter that gave the reader additional information.'

4.note: OF Blog raw page reached (HTTP 200); page header confirms 'Monday, April 28, 2003 / Robin Hobb Interview', matching the 2003 attribution. Q14: 'It was horribly inconvenient at times, because I could never say, "Meanwhile, back at the castle, thus and so was happening." I could only tell the reader what Fitz knew at that moment.' Both limbs supported.

5.note: Quote exact; page: 'In the Liveship books, I had a storyline where important events were occurring simultaneously in different places. Rather than limit the story to one person's experience... I decided to use third person and write from several points-of-view.' Simultaneity is the only reason the page gives for the switch, so the claim's 'only' stands; note the page also cites a second benefit (multiple perspectives on one event) as a consequence, not a cause.

6.trueWording: drags that same baggage through the reading
6.note: Quote exact; full support: 'When my characters get hurt, physically or emotionally, they acquire baggage and later on it may affect what they do. As the reader experiences the story, he drags that same baggage through the reading.' Claim's 'alters' is slightly firmer than the page's 'may affect'.

7.trueWording: they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on
7.note: Quote exact and the first half is fully supported: 'many fantasy tales where the heroes or heroines endure some truly awful experiences, but they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on, and in some cases, it doesn't seem to have lingering effects or change the character in any way.' Two gaps: (a) the page hedges 'in some cases' where the claim asserts flatly that such events leave no lingering change; (b) the page nowhere says Hobb dwells on the event - the nearest wording is 'the character experiences them deeply and thus the reader feels those events more strongly.' 'Lets it change the character' is supported by the adjacent baggage paragraph; the dwelling limb is inference.
7.unsupportedLimb: that Hobb herself dwells on the event - the page says only that her characters experience events deeply

8.trueWording: perceived as more harrowing or depressing
8.note: Quote exact. Denial limb: 'I don't think my characters endure anything that is more harrowing than, for example, the members of the Fellowship in the Lord of the Rings' and 'I don't think that I do exceptionally cruel things to my characters.' Lived-from-inside limb: the Boromir example, 'we would perceive his torment and his torn loyalties a lot more sharply than we do when we only see his actions.' Page names the Fellowship/LOTR rather than Tolkien by name.

9.note: Fantasy Book Critic raw page reached (HTTP 200); header confirms 'Monday, January 7, 2008 / Interview with Robin Hobb'. Page: 'I would describe my writing style as both leisurely and intimate.' Answering a direct question about her own style, so 'her own style, in two words' is exact.

10.trueWording: usually a lot slower than towards the end
10.note: Quote exact: 'The pacing at the beginning of any of my books is usually a lot slower than towards the end of the book, simply because so many words are given over to character construction.' The 'simply because...' clause carries the claim's 'deliberately'. The claim drops the page's 'usually' hedge, though the quote itself retains it.

11.trueWording: construct the ramps up to that exciting scene
11.note: Quote exact and every limb present: 'when I didn't slow down and construct the ramps up to that exciting scene, when I propelled the reader directly into it, it lacked the impact and significance I wanted it to have.'

12.note: Quote is an exact contiguous substring (page reads 'may not directly'). For me, that means putting in details and incidents that...'
